Fair Labor Standards Amendments of 1989 - Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (the Act) to increase the minimum wage per hour from $3.35 in 1989 to: (1) $3.85 in 1990; (2) $4.25 in 1991; and (3) $4.65 in 1992 and thereafter.

Provides for biennial adjustments of the minimum wage beginning in 1994. Directs the Minimum Wage Review Board (established by this Act), during the 90-day period beginning January 1, 1994, to review current economic data on wages, prices, and other economic indicators and determine how the minimum wage rate should be adjusted. Directs the Board, by October 1, 1994, to transmit to the Congress a recommendation of the rate that should be placed in effect on January 1, 1995, including an estimate of the economic effects of doing so. Directs the Board to conduct such reviews and transmit such recommendations biennially.

Establishes the Minimum Wage Review Board, composed of five members appointed by the President and certain congressional officers.

Increases the small business exemption by revising the definition of an enterprise engaged in commerce for purposes of coverage under the Act ("the enterprise test"). Exempts from such coverage retail or service establishments whose annual gross volume of sales or business is less than $500,000 (currently $362,500), effective in 1989. Requires employers who were covered in 1988, but who are exempt under the new threshold, to continue to pay the $3.35 per hour minimum wage.

Increases the tip credit under the Act from 40 percent to 45 percent for 1990 and to 50 percent for 1991 and thereafter. (The tip credit deems the amount paid to a tipped employee, for minimum wage purposes, to be increased by an amount determined by the employer, but not by an amount in excess of the specified percentage of the applicable minimum wage rate.)

Directs the Board, by October 1, 1992, to transmit to the Congress a recommendation to adjust the rate, including an estimate of the economic effects of doing so. Directs the Board to conduct such reviews and transmit such recommendations annually.

Requires employers who were covered in 1988, but who are exempt under the new threshold, to continue to pay the $3.35 per hour minimum wage (and continue to be covered by overtime and child labor provisions of the Act).

Increases the tip credit under the Act from 40 percent to 45 percent for 1990 and to 50 percent for 1991 and thereafter. (The tip credit deems the amount paid to a tipped employee, for minimum wage purposes, to be increased by an amount determined by the employer, but not by an amount in excess of the specified percentage of the applicable minimum wage rate.)

Applies rights and protections under the Act to any employee in an employment position in, and any employing authority of, the House of Representatives, using remedies and procedures under the Fair Employment Practices Resolution.

Removes the Virgin Islands from coverage by provisions for special industry committee minimum wage determinations and orders, including those involving employment under special certificates for learners, apprentices, and messengers and for students. Adds references to American Samoa under such provisions (American Samoa is currently covered by such provisions through references under other special minimum wage provisions). Removes references to Puerto Rico under such provisions, but continues and revises the special minimum wage treatment of Puerto Rico as follows: (1) in addition to designated types of employees (Federal, hotel, motel, restaurant, and food service) entitled to receive the full Federal minimum wage, employees in industries averaging $4.65 or more per hour would be so entitled; (2) employees in industries averaging from $4.00 to $4.64 per hour would receive the full rate in 1994 after a five-year period of gradual increases; (3) employees in industries averaging less than $4.00 per hour would receive the full rate in 1995 after a six-year period of gradual increases; and (4) employees of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or a municipality or other governmental entity of the Commonwealth, in categories averaging less than $4.00 per hour and covered by 1985 amendments to the Act, would receive the full rate in 1996 after a seven-year period of gradual increases.

Directs the Board, by October 1, 1992, to transmit to the Congress a recommendation to adjust the rate, including an estimate of the economic effects of doing so. Directs the Board to conduct such reviews and transmit such recommendations annually.

Applies the rights and protections under the Act to any employee in an employment position in, and any employing authority of, the House of Representatives, using remedies and procedures under the Fair Employment Practices Resolution.

Allows employers to pay a training wage at less than the minimum wage rate. Allows such training wage to be paid to eligible employees who have not previously worked for the employer or any other employer and who are not employed in agriculture. Limits payment of the training wage to 60 days beginning on the day the employee begins employment, during the period from October 1, 1989, to September 30, 1992.

Sets such training wage at: (1) not less than $3.35 per hour during FY 1990; and (2) during FY 1991, not less than $3.35 per hour or 85 percent of the minimum wage, whichever is greater. Prohibits layoffs or terminations of employment or reduction of the number of regular employees because of the training wage. Directs the Secretary of Labor to report to the Congress by January 1, 1993, on the effectiveness of the training wage.

Title I: Minimum Wage Restoration Act of 1989 - Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to increase the Federal minimum wage per hour from $3.35 to: (1) $3.85 in FY 1990; (2) $4.25 in FY 1991; and (3) $4.55 in FY 1992 and thereafter.

Adds references to American Samoa under such provisions (American Samoa is currently covered by references under other special minimum wage provisions). Removes references to Puerto Rico under such provisions, but continues and revises the special minimum wage treatment of Puerto Rico as follows: (1) in addition to designated types of employees (Federal, hotel, motel, restaurant, and food service) entitled to receive the full Federal minimum wage, employees in industries averaging $4.55 or more per hour would be so entitled; (2) employees in industries averaging from $4.00 to $4.64 per hour would receive the full rate by October 1, 1993, after a four-year period of gradual increases; (3) employees in industries averaging less than $4.00 per hour would receive the full rate by October 1, 1994, after a five-year period of gradual increases; and (4) employees of the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or a municipality or other governmental entity of the Commonwealth, in categories averaging less than $4.00 per hour and covered by 1985 amendments to the Act, would receive the full rate by October 1, 1995, after a six-year period of gradual increases.

Increases the tip credit under the Act from 40 percent to 45 percent for FY 1990 and to 50 percent for FY 1991 and thereafter. (The tip credit deems the amount paid to a tipped employee, for minimum wage purposes, to be increased by an amount determined by the employer, but not by an amount in excess of the specified percentage of the applicable minimum wage rate.)

Allows employers to pay a training wage at less than the minimum wage rate. Allows the training wage to be paid to eligible employees who: (1) have not previously worked for an employer or employers in employment for which payroll taxes have been withheld; and (2) are not migrant or seasonal agricultural workers. Allows such training wage to be paid only to an eligible employee engaged in on-the-day training who has not worked 30 days with one such employer, or 60 days with one such employer, or 60 days with all such employers. Makes the individual responsible for providing proof of previous periods of employment with other employers. Allows such training wage to be paid only during the period from October 1, 1989, to September 30, 1992. Sets such training wage at: (1) not less than $3.35 per hour during the year beginning October 1, 1989; and (2) beginning October 1, 1990, not less than $3.35 per hour or 85 percent of the minimum wage, whichever is greater. Prohibits layoffs or termination of employment or reduction of the number of regular employees because of the training wage. Prohibits employee hours at the training wage during any month from exceeding one-fourth of all employee hours in the establishment. Sets forth notice requirements and enforcement provisions. Directs the Secretary of Labor (the Secretary) to report to the Congress by July 1, 1992, on the effectiveness of the training wage.

Exempts from overtime provisions of the Act up to ten hours in any workweek if during such time the employee is receiving certain remedial education.

Expresses the sense of the Senate that the rights and protections of the Act should apply to employees of the Senate or any office thereof. Directs the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration, within 180 days after the first minimum wage increase under this Act, to report a resolution which applies such rights and protection to Senate employees and establishes the scope of such coverage and remedies, enforcement, and other necessary procedures.

Expresses the sense of the Senate that the United States, in addition to increasing the minimum wage, should deal with the problems of working poor families by taking additional measures, including: (1) in the long term, improving their access to education, training, quality health care, and child care; and (2) in the short term, providing for a family-size adjusted earned income credit.

Directs each congressional committee that reports legislation which requires employers to provide new employee benefits or otherwise affects employment levels and conditions to: (1) seek objective analysis of the impact of such legislation on employment, economic competitiveness, economic growth, the Federal budget, and international trade; and (2) include such analysis in its committee report.

Modifies the overtime exemption for employees of irrigation districts which handle water exclusively for agricultural purposes.

Directs the Secretary to: (1) study the impact of the minimum wage increases on rural areas and high unemployment areas, considering specified factors, and the feasibility of establishing a minimum wage differential for such areas; and (2) report to specified congressional committees by June 1, 1991.

Directs the Secretary, within 90 days, to promulgate regulations that interpret a specified professional exemption from overtime provisions under the Act to include computer systems analysts, software engineers, and other similarly skilled professional workers, even if such employees are compensated on an hourly basis, as long as they are compensated at an hourly rate at least six and one-half times greater than the minimum.

Directs the Secretary to conduct surveys and research on the characteristics of minimum wage employment and the impact of the modification to the scope of coverage and minimum wage levels, including specified studies which are to be completed by certain deadlines, and to make the results available to the Congress.

Expresses the sense of the Senate with respect to, and requests the House of Representatives to adopt and send to the Senate, a bill repealing or substantially modifying specified provisions of the Internal Revenue Code (the nondiscrimination requirement provisions (Internal Revenue Code section 89)) which limit the differences in health and other nontaxable benefits an employer may provide as tax-deductible compensation for employees.

Adds civil penalties for repeated or willful violations of specified provisions of the Act.

Title II: Earnings Test - Amends title II (Old Age, Survivors and Disability Insurance) of the Social Security Act to revise the social security retirement test (under which benefits are reduced when earnings exceed certain levels). Increases the amount of earnings a beneficiary age 65 to 69 may have before such reductions take place. Eliminates provisions which allow certain persons to claim up to six months of retroactive benefits for months of eligibility prior to age 65.

Expresses the sense of the Senate that: (1) the amount of such exempted earnings be further increased incrementally during the period of 1990 to 2000 and the earnings test limitation be repealed by the year 2000 for those who have attained the retirement age of 65; and (2) a specified delayed retirement credit be fully implemented by the year 2000.

Expresses the sense of the Senate that the Senate Finance Committee review and hold hearings on the Medicare Catastrophic Coverage Act of 1988, including its financing mechanism.
